findings.title: Redeem path never re-derives the shares-mint PDA, allowing a spoofed vault/mint pair to burn an unrelated mint while draining vault assets

content.summary: `RedeemSharesContext::validate` checks only that the supplied `shares_mint` account key equals the `vault.shares_mint` field read out of the vault account's own bytes; it never calls `VaultSharesMint::check_vault` to re-derive the canonical PDA from seeds `[SHARES_MINT, vault_info.key, vault.vault_shares_mint_bump]`, unlike `DepositContext::validate`. Combined with `VaultInfo::try_from`/`validate` omitting the vault account owner check, the enforced equality reduces to attacker-supplied data agreeing with itself, so a redeemer can present a mint that is not the vault's canonical shares mint and still have the handler succeed.
content.description:
The rule `rule_redeem_shares_mint_is_canonical_pda` asserts that any successful `process_redeem_shares` implies `accounts[3].key == create_vault_shares_mint_address(accounts[0].key, &vault)`. The Prover refuted it: the trace reaches `process_redeem_shares` → `RedeemSharesContext::load` → `RedeemSharesContext::validate`, passes through validation with no error return, and reaches the user assertion at `redemption.rs:508` with the pre-computed boolean `key_is_canonical_pda: '0'` — i.e. the supplied shares-mint key and the seed-derived address genuinely differ on a successful execution with `amount = 1`.

The structural root cause is readable directly in the source and does not depend on the prover's numeric modelling. `RedeemSharesContext::validate` in `programs/vault/src/loaders/vault_loaders.rs` performs exactly three equality checks:

```rust
require_eq!(&vault.assets_mint,  self.assets_mint.key,          ...);
require_eq!(&vault.shares_mint,  self.shares_mint.as_ref().key, ...);
require_eq!(&vault.vault_assets_account, self.vault_assets_account.key, ...);
```

The middle check ties the supplied account only to the `vault.shares_mint` *field stored inside the vault account's bytes*. No derivation is performed anywhere on the redeem path. The helper that would do it, `VaultSharesMint::check_vault` (which calls `create_vault_shares_mint_address` and compares against the account key), exists on the type and is invoked by `DepositContext::validate`, but is never called from `RedeemSharesContext::validate`; `VaultSharesMint::validate` is merely `Ok(self)`. So the asserted property is not just false on a particular witness — it is unestablishable, because nothing in the handler ever establishes it, and no later code can reject the account either.

This compounds with a second gap: `VaultInfo::try_from` → `validate` only calls `Vault::validate`, which is a single `require_ne!(assets_mint, shares_mint)`. The vault account's owner is never checked (the comment promising an owner check is not implemented), there is no account-type discriminant, and no length check before the `bytemuck::from_bytes` cast. Consequently both `vault.shares_mint` and `vault.vault_shares_mint_bump` are read out of a buffer an attacker can fully control, and the one equality that *is* enforced degenerates to supplied data agreeing with itself.

The same omission applies to the vault assets account on this path: `RedeemSharesContext` stores `vault_assets_account` as a bare `AccountInfo`, so `VaultAssetsAccount::check_vault` is not even reachable from it, while the unvalidated bump from that same buffer is what `vault_assets_account_seeds_with_bump!` feeds to `invoke_signed`.

The practical consequence matches the property's own wording: the burn CPI destroys tokens of a mint unrelated to the vault's real shares, while the redeemer is still credited with vault assets.
content.impact: An attacker can redeem against the vault while the burn CPI targets a mint that is not the vault's canonical shares mint — burning worthless attacker-controlled tokens instead of genuine vault shares, yet still receiving vault assets out. Because the real shares supply is left untouched, the vault's asset backing is drained while outstanding legitimate shares remain, making remaining shareholders' claims unbacked and the vault insolvent.
content.attack_path:
1. Attacker constructs a vault-shaped account buffer whose `shares_mint` field names an attacker-controlled mint and whose `assets_mint` differs from it (satisfying the only check in `Vault::validate`), with a `vault_shares_mint_bump` of the attacker's choosing. `VaultInfo::try_from` accepts it because the owner, discriminant, and length are never checked.
2. Attacker calls `process_redeem_shares` with `amount > 0`, passing this vault at index 0 and the attacker-controlled mint at index 3.
3. `RedeemSharesContext::validate` compares `vault.shares_mint` to the supplied mint key — they match, since both are attacker-chosen — and returns Ok. `VaultSharesMint::check_vault` is never called, so the seed-derived canonical PDA is never computed or compared (`key_is_canonical_pda: '0'` in the counterexample).
4. The handler proceeds: the burn CPI destroys tokens of the unrelated attacker mint, and the asset transfer, signed via `vault_assets_account_seeds_with_bump!` using the same unvalidated bump, credits the redeemer with vault assets.
content.assumptions_and_uncertainties: The prover summarizes `Pubkey::create_program_address`, so `expected` is an unconstrained value; a rule of this shape would report VIOLATED whether or not the derivation check existed. The verdict is therefore consistent with the defect but is not independent evidence of it — the evidence is the source of `RedeemSharesContext::validate`, which contains no derivation. The trace also carries seven `BWOr` imprecision notes around the pubkey reads and reports `canonical_shares_mint_pda_lo64` as a 256-bit value outside `u64` range; those numeric artefacts are a reason to distrust the printed witness pubkeys, but not the structural conclusion, which depends on no number. Full exploitability additionally assumes an attacker can satisfy the remaining downstream SPL Token constraints (notably burn authority over their own mint and the vault assets account's signed transfer), which the model does not fully exercise.

provenance.risk_reasoning: The missing `check_vault` call is unconditional — every redeem goes through the same three field-equality checks and no derivation — and the absent vault owner/discriminant validation lets an attacker supply a self-consistent fake vault buffer, so no privileged access is needed. Likelihood is medium rather than high because the attacker must assemble a consistent set of spoofed accounts (vault buffer, mint, assets account) and the funded vault assets account must still authorize the transfer; impact is high because the result is unbacked asset withdrawal and vault insolvency.

findings.title: Redeem path never re-derives the vault assets PDA, letting a forged vault account steer the program's invoke_signed transfer

content.summary: `RedeemSharesContext::validate` only checks that the supplied `vault_assets_account` key equals the `vault.vault_assets_account` field read out of the vault account's own (unvalidated) bytes; it never re-derives the canonical `[VAULT_ASSETS, vault_info.key, bump]` PDA the way `DepositContext` and `SlashContext` do via `VaultAssetsAccount::check_vault`. The Certora Prover produced an accepted `process_redeem_shares` execution in which `key_is_canonical_pda = 0`, i.e. the account the handler later signs an asset transfer out of is not the program's canonical assets PDA.
content.description:
Property 8 requires that a successful `process_redeem_shares` implies the account at index 1 — the account out of which the handler signs an SPL transfer with `invoke_signed` using `vault_assets_account_seeds_with_bump!` — equals the address derived from `[VAULT_ASSETS, vault_info.key, vault.vault_assets_account_bump]` under `crate::ID`.

`RedeemSharesContext::validate` (programs/vault/src/loaders/vault_loaders.rs) performs exactly three equality checks:

```rust
require_eq!(&vault.assets_mint,          self.assets_mint.key,          ...);
require_eq!(&vault.shares_mint,          self.shares_mint.as_ref().key, ...);
require_eq!(&vault.vault_assets_account, self.vault_assets_account.key, ...);
```

The third ties the passed account only to the `vault_assets_account` field stored inside the vault account's bytes. It never calls `create_vault_assets_account_address`. The helper that does this, `VaultAssetsAccount::check_vault`, exists on the type and is invoked by both `DepositContext::validate` and `SlashContext::validate`, but `RedeemSharesContext` holds its `vault_assets_account` as a bare `AccountInfo`, so the check is not even reachable from this context. There is therefore no line of code on the redeem path relating `accounts[1].key` to the seed-derived address — the property is not merely false on an adversarial witness, it is unestablishable.

The counterexample confirms this on an accepted execution: with `amount = 1` (so the non-degenerate branch), the trace runs `process_redeem_shares` → `RedeemSharesContext::load` → `RedeemSharesContext::validate` with no error return, and then fails the rule's own assertion at redemption.rs:462. The decisive logged artifact is `key_is_canonical_pda: '0'`, computed from the same direct `Pubkey` comparison the assertion reads: the handler accepted and ran to completion with `accounts[1].key != expected`. (The `Pk` renderings and the `pk_lo64` values in the trace are degraded by `BWOr` imprecision in the logging helper only; those values are not read by the assertion or by the boolean.)

The defect compounds with weak validation of the vault account itself. `VaultInfo::try_from` → `validate` only calls `Vault::validate`, which checks `assets_mint != shares_mint` and nothing more — no owner check, no discriminant, no data-length check, despite the comments in `try_from` claiming "owned by vault program / has discriminant". Both `vault.vault_assets_account` and `vault.vault_assets_account_bump` are read out of that unvalidated buffer, and the bump is fed straight into the signer seeds of the `invoke_signed` that moves assets. An attacker presenting a look-alike vault account thus chooses both the account the program treats as its assets PDA and the seeds it signs with, and the surviving `require_eq!` degenerates into the attacker's own data agreeing with itself.

Remediation: change `RedeemSharesContext::vault_assets_account` to a typed `VaultAssetsAccount<'info>` (matching Deposit/Slash) and add `self.vault_assets_account.check_vault(self.vault_info.as_ref().key, &vault)?;` to `validate`; likewise call `self.shares_mint.check_vault(...)` for the shares mint; and give `VaultInfo::try_from`/`validate` the owner check, account-type discriminant, and data-length check its comments already promise. The re-derivation and the vault-account validation interlock — re-deriving from an attacker-chosen bump in an attacker-owned buffer is not a check.
content.impact: The program can be induced to sign, with its own PDA authority, an SPL token transfer out of an account that is not its canonical vault assets PDA, with seeds the attacker supplies. Combined with the missing owner/discriminant validation on the vault account, this breaks the core custody invariant of the redeem path and puts vault assets (or assets of any account for which the attacker can get the program to produce a valid signer) at risk of misdirection or loss.
content.attack_path:
1. Attacker constructs a vault-like account (owner and discriminant are never checked by `VaultInfo::try_from`/`Vault::validate`, which only enforces `assets_mint != shares_mint`), populating `assets_mint`, `shares_mint`, `vault_assets_account`, and `vault_assets_account_bump` with values of their choosing.
2. Attacker calls `process_redeem_shares` with `amount > 0`, passing that vault account at index 0 and, at index 1, the non-canonical token account named in the forged `vault_assets_account` field.
3. `RedeemSharesContext::load`/`validate` succeed: the three `require_eq!` checks compare the passed mints and assets account against the attacker's own vault bytes, which agree by construction, and no PDA re-derivation occurs.
4. The handler reads `vault_assets_account_bump` back from the same attacker-controlled buffer and feeds it to `vault_assets_account_seeds_with_bump!` as signer seeds for the `invoke_signed` asset transfer — signing out of an account that is not the canonical `[VAULT_ASSETS, vault_info.key, bump]` PDA (`key_is_canonical_pda = 0` in the trace).
content.assumptions_and_uncertainties: The Prover summarizes `Pubkey::create_program_address`, so the derived `expected` address in the counterexample is an unconstrained value rather than a faithful hash of the seeds; the specific numbers in the trace are therefore not themselves evidence of a reachable on-chain derivation, and no witness under this configuration could be. The finding rests on the structural absence of the derivation in `RedeemSharesContext::validate`, which is independent of the witness values. The `BWOr` imprecision warnings and the `MAX_UINT256` / `2^256 - 14` renderings affect only the rule's byte-reassembly logging helper, not the assertion or the `key_is_canonical_pda` boolean. Full end-to-end exploitation also depends on the missing owner/discriminant validation in `VaultInfo::try_from`, which is reported here as part of the same root cause; the missing `shares_mint.check_vault` on this path is noted but tracked separately.

provenance.risk_reasoning: The missing check is structural and readable in the source — the redeem path contains no derivation of the assets PDA at all, unlike deposit and slash — and the prover reached the assertion on an execution where load/validate completed cleanly with key_is_canonical_pda = 0. Likelihood is medium rather than high because the Prover summarizes Pubkey::create_program_address, so the specific witness pubkeys are unconstrained and are not themselves proof of a concrete on-chain derivation; exploitation requires crafting a look-alike vault account whose self-consistent fields the unvalidated VaultInfo::try_from will accept.

findings.title: Permissionless `process_update_reward` can credit donated assets to a share-less vault, permanently bricking deposits and stranding the tokens

content.summary: `process_update_reward` syncs the vault's recorded `assets` to the SPL token account balance without ever checking that shares are outstanding. Anyone can donate tokens to the vault's asset account and call this signer-less handler, moving a freshly initialized vault from `(shares = 0, assets = 0)` to `(shares = 0, assets > 0)`. In that state every deposit computes zero shares and reverts in `mint_shares`, and no shares exist to redeem, so the vault is bricked and the donated tokens are permanently stranded.
content.description:
The rule `rule_update_reward_no_assets_with_zero_shares` assumed an entry state of `vault.shares == 0` and `vault.assets == 0` with genuine account ownership (`assume_real_owners!`: vault owned by `crate::ID`, asset account owned by `spl_token::id()`), and asked whether a successful `process_update_reward` can leave `assets > 0` while `shares == 0`. The Prover produced a concrete, fully successful counterexample: with the asset token account holding a balance of `3` (decoded by the program's own `spl_token_account_amount` → `<spl_token::state::Account as Pack>::unpack_from_slice`), the handler returned `Ok` and the post-state is `shares = 0`, `assets = 3`, failing `cvlr_assert!(a1 == 0)` at `reward_accounting.rs:446`.

Root cause, entirely in program code:

- `UpdateRewardContext::load` validates only `Vault::validate` (which is just `require_ne!(assets_mint, shares_mint)`) and `require_eq!(&vault.vault_assets_account, self.vault_assets_account.key)`. The account list contains **no signer**, so the instruction is permissionless, and the asset account is not re-derived/pinned the way `DepositContext::validate` and `SlashContext::validate` do with `VaultAssetsAccount::check_vault`.
- `crate::operations::vault_update_reward` computes `reward = new_amt.checked_sub(vault.num_assets())` and calls `vault.add_token(reward)` when `reward > 0`.
- `Vault::add_token` checks only `require_gt!(amt, 0)` and the `checked_add`. **Nothing on this path consults `vault.shares`**, so a reward can be recognized against an empty share base.

The resulting state is terminal:

- A subsequent deposit calls `Vault::convert_assets_to_shares`. With `shares = 0` and `assets = 3`, the `num_shares() == num_assets()` 1:1 passthrough branch does not fire (0 ≠ 3), so it computes `mul_div_floor(token, 0, 3) = 0`, and `Vault::mint_shares(0)` is rejected by `require_gt!(amt, 0, VaultError::GuardFail)`. Every deposit, of every size, reverts.
- `vault_redeem_shares` burns shares, and there are no shares outstanding to burn, so redemption cannot recover the tokens either.

Note the damaging state was *created by the handler itself* — the rule pinned both `s0 == 0` and `a0 == 0` on entry — so this is not a case of a vault that was already broken. Pre- and post-state reads go through the same zero-copy `bytemuck::from_bytes` cast that `VaultInfo::get` performs, and the balance used came from the program's own helper, so there is no harness artifact to blame. The witness balance of `3` is an ordinary, plainly representable value rather than an arithmetic edge case.

Recommended remediation (for the protocol authors):
1. In `vault_update_reward`, require `vault.num_shares() > 0` before calling `add_token(reward)`, returning `VaultError::GuardFail` otherwise — this forecloses the counterexample's transition outright.
2. Optionally/complementarily, give `convert_assets_to_shares` a defined bootstrap branch for `shares == 0` so a depositor can absorb donated assets instead of being turned away (weigh this against inflation-attack surface, which is presumably why `deposit_exact` exists).
3. As defence in depth, restrict who can drive the sync: require an authority signature on `process_update_reward`, or at minimum pin the asset account with `VaultAssetsAccount::check_vault`. This mitigates exposure but does not fix the state machine, so it should accompany (1) or (2) rather than replace them.

If (1) is adopted, any specification asserting unconditional success of the reward path for `balance > assets` must be restated to carry the `shares > 0` precondition.
content.impact: The vault is permanently bricked for the affected configuration: with `shares == 0` and `assets > 0`, every deposit reverts inside `mint_shares` (zero shares computed) and no shares exist to redeem, so the vault can never accept funds again and the donated tokens are irrecoverably stranded in the asset account. For a freshly initialized or fully-exited vault this is a cheap, permanent denial of service — the counterexample used a balance of just 3 token units — and any tokens donated or otherwise sitting in the account at that moment are frozen.
content.attack_path:
1. A vault exists in the empty state `(shares = 0, assets = 0)` — e.g. freshly initialized, or after all shares have been redeemed.
2. The attacker transfers a trivial amount of the asset token (the counterexample uses 3 units) directly into the vault's asset token account. No permission is needed; SPL token accounts accept transfers from anyone.
3. The attacker invokes `process_update_reward` with the vault and its asset account. `UpdateRewardContext::load` passes (mints differ, the asset account key matches `vault.vault_assets_account`) and no signer is required.
4. `vault_update_reward` computes `reward = 3 - 0 = 3` and `Vault::add_token(3)` succeeds, since neither function consults `vault.shares`.
5. The vault is now `(shares = 0, assets = 3)`. Every later deposit hits `convert_assets_to_shares`, misses the 1:1 passthrough branch (0 ≠ 3), computes `mul_div_floor(token, 0, 3) = 0`, and reverts in `mint_shares` on `require_gt!(amt, 0)`. No shares exist to redeem, so the 3 tokens are stranded forever.
content.assumptions_and_uncertainties: The finding assumes the vault can legitimately be in or reach the `(shares = 0, assets = 0)` state, which is the natural post-initialization state and also arises after a full redemption. The counterexample relies on realistic ownership only (`assume_real_owners!`), not on forged accounts. One alternative reading is that syncing `assets` to the balance is exactly the handler's job, so forbidding `assets > 0` at `shares == 0` is stricter than its contract — but that relocates rather than removes the bug, since nothing in `process_update_reward`, `UpdateRewardContext`, `vault_update_reward`, `add_token`, or `convert_assets_to_shares` prevents entry into the state or allows exit from it. This single trace speaks only to this rule; it implies nothing about the status of the other rules in the batch (fee-backing, owner checks, dilution, solvency, reachability), none of which should be cited as corroboration.

provenance.risk_reasoning: Both steps are permissionless and require no privileged access: SPL token accounts accept transfers from anyone, and `UpdateRewardContext::load` requires no signer and only checks mint inequality plus the stored asset-account pubkey. The cost is a few token units (the counterexample used a balance of 3), and the resulting state is unrecoverable through any code path in the program, permanently freezing the assets and disabling deposits.

findings.title: `vault_update_reward` reconciles against `vault.assets` instead of `gross_assets()`, double-counting pending fees as shareholder reward and breaking fee backing

content.summary: `vault_update_reward` computes the recognized reward as `token_balance - vault.assets`, ignoring `vault.fee_amount` even though pending fees are custodied in the very same `vault_assets_account` and are later paid out by `collect_fee`. The Prover refuted the backing invariant `vault.assets + vault.fee_amount <= balance(vault_assets_account)`: with `assets = 4808` and `fee_amount = 1` at entry, a successful `process_update_reward` leaves `assets == balance` while `fee_amount = 1` is still outstanding, so the pending fee has been credited a second time to shareholders.
content.description:
The vault's asset token account is the custody account for two distinct claims: the shareholder claim tracked in `vault.assets`, and the pending protocol fee tracked in `vault.fee_amount`. The state type already encodes this: `Vault::gross_assets()` is defined as `assets + fee_amount` precisely because both are backed by the same pot, and `vault_collect_fee` transfers `fee_amount` tokens out of that same account.

`vault_update_reward` (programs/vault/src/operations/vault_operations.rs) is the single place in the program that reconciles recorded state against the real on-chain balance, and it reconciles against the wrong quantity:

```rust
let reward = new_amt
    .checked_sub(vault.num_assets())
    .ok_or(VaultError::MathOverflow)?;
if reward > 0 { vault.add_token(reward)?; }
```

Only `vault.assets` is deducted. Any tokens sitting in the account to back an uncollected fee are therefore treated as surplus — i.e. as reward — and credited to shareholders via `add_token`. The result is a double count: the same tokens now back both `vault.assets` and `vault.fee_amount`.

`rule_update_reward_preserves_fee_backing` formalizes the backing invariant. On a well-shaped, program-owned vault state account and a 165-byte `spl_token`-owned asset account with distinct keys, it assumes `vault.assets + vault.fee_amount <= balance(vault_assets_account)` at entry, calls `process_update_reward` with `.unwrap()` (so only successful executions are covered), and asserts the same inequality afterwards. The Prover produced an execution where it fails, at reward_accounting.rs:329.

In the counterexample the entry state is `a0 = vault.assets = 4808`, `f0 = vault.fee_amount = 1`, and a token balance `bal0` that comfortably satisfies `4808 + 1 <= bal0` (the solver happened to pick a very large `u64` near `u64::MAX`; the magnitude is incidental). `UpdateRewardContext::load` and `spl_token_account_amount` both complete, the handler returns `Ok`, and no transfer occurs — `bal1 == bal0`. The post-state is `a1 == bal1` (assets inflated to the entire token balance) with `f1 = 1` unchanged, so the postcondition degenerates to `bal0 + 1 <= bal0` and fails.

The break is structural rather than an artifact of the chosen witness: whenever the handler succeeds with `fee_amount > 0` and a strictly positive reward, `assets` is set to the full balance while the fee claim remains outstanding, so `assets + fee_amount <= balance` cannot hold. Notably this is not an arithmetic overflow — both `checked_sub` and `checked_add` succeed; the subtraction simply uses the wrong operand. It is also invisible to the program's own `Vault::check_invariant`, which only checks `shares <= assets` and is unaffected because `assets` only grows here.

The downstream consequence is a solvency gap: once the admin calls `collect_fee`, `fee_amount` tokens leave the asset account while `vault.assets` is not reduced, leaving the vault recording more assets than it actually holds, so not all redemptions can be honoured.

Note also that the related Property 1 formulation — "after a successful call, `vault.assets` equals exactly the token balance" — is itself a symptom of the same omission; it is only correct while `fee_amount == 0` and would need restating in gross form (`assets + fee_amount == balance`) once the handler is fixed.

Recommended fix: compute the reward against all outstanding claims, i.e. `new_amt.checked_sub(vault.gross_assets())` instead of `new_amt.checked_sub(vault.num_assets())`. This recognizes only the genuine surplus, keeps the pending fee backed, and has the useful side effect that a balance below `assets + fee_amount` now fails `checked_sub` and returns `MathOverflow`, which is the correct response to a real shortfall. More broadly, every comparison of the asset account's balance against recorded state should use `gross_assets()`.
content.impact: Pending protocol fees are recognized a second time as shareholder reward, inflating `vault.assets` to the full token balance while `fee_amount` remains owed. A subsequent `collect_fee` then moves those same tokens out of the asset account without reducing `vault.assets`, leaving the vault recording more assets than it custodies — shares are over-valued and the last redeemers cannot be paid in full. This is a direct accounting/solvency defect affecting user funds, not merely a cosmetic deviation.
content.attack_path:
1. The vault holds a non-zero pending fee in `vault.fee_amount` (counterexample: `fee_amount = 1`, `assets = 4808`), backed by tokens sitting in `vault_assets_account` alongside the shareholder assets; the backing invariant `assets + fee_amount <= balance` holds.
2. Anyone calls the reward-sync instruction, `process_update_reward`. The handler loads the context, reads the real token balance via `spl_token_account_amount`, and computes `reward = balance - vault.assets` — which includes the tokens earmarked for the pending fee.
3. `vault.add_token(reward)` credits that amount to shareholders. The post-state is `vault.assets == balance` with `vault.fee_amount` still outstanding; the backing invariant is now violated (`assert FAIL` at reward_accounting.rs:329).
4. The admin later calls `collect_fee`, which transfers `fee_amount` tokens out of `vault_assets_account` and clears the counter without reducing `vault.assets`. The vault now records more assets than it holds, and redemptions can no longer all be honoured.
content.assumptions_and_uncertainties: The counterexample requires `vault.fee_amount > 0` at entry. In the exact code snapshot audited, no handler ever *increases* `vault.fee_amount` — the only writer is `Vault::clear_fee_amount` called from `vault_collect_fee`, and the fee-based deposit paths route fees to a separate fee token account rather than crediting the counter. The defect in `vault_update_reward` is therefore real at the code level but latent as an exploit against this snapshot; it becomes live as soon as fee accrual onto `vault.fee_amount` is wired up, which the existence of the field, `gross_assets()` and `collect_fee` all plainly anticipate. The rule's only assumptions beyond account shape, key distinctness and realistic ownership are the entry backing invariant itself, so nothing in the harness manufactures the failure.

findings.title: process_update_reward reads the vault asset balance from an account whose owner is never checked, letting a forged token account inflate vault.assets

content.summary: `UpdateRewardContext` validates only that the supplied asset account's *key* matches `vault.vault_assets_account`; neither the loader nor `spl_token_account_amount` verifies that the account is owned by the SPL Token program. The Prover produced an execution in which `process_update_reward` returns `Ok` after unpacking a 165-byte buffer owned by a non-Token program and crediting the decoded balance as reward, raising the persisted `vault.assets` from 22443 to a different, attacker-chosen value.
content.description:
The reward-sync path reads the vault's asset balance straight out of an `AccountInfo` buffer without ever establishing that the buffer is genuine SPL Token state.

Three gaps compose into the defect:

1. `UpdateRewardContext::validate` (programs/vault/src/loaders/vault_loaders.rs) contains exactly one guard for this account: `require_eq!(&vault.vault_assets_account, self.vault_assets_account.key, ProgramError::InvalidArgument)`. That is a key comparison only — it never consults `info.owner`. The field is declared as a bare `AccountInfo<'info>` rather than `VaultAssetsAccount<'info>`, so even the existing `VaultAssetsAccount::check_vault` helper is unreachable here (and `check_vault` only re-derives a PDA, which would still not establish ownership). Unlike `DepositContext::validate` and `SlashContext::validate`, `UpdateRewardContext` does not call it at all.

2. `spl_token_account_amount` (programs/vault/src/processor/spl_token_utils.rs) is just `spl_token::state::Account::unpack(&info.try_borrow_data()?)` followed by `Ok(account.amount)`. `Pack::unpack` validates the buffer length, the `COption` discriminant tags and the `is_initialized` flag — it cannot validate `info.owner`, because it is handed a byte slice, not an account. Any 165-byte buffer whose bytes happen to parse yields an `amount`.

3. `vault_update_reward` then takes that caller-chosen number as `new_amt`, computes `reward = new_amt - vault.assets`, and calls `add_token(reward)`. Nothing downstream re-checks provenance.

The counterexample exercises exactly this path. The asset account in slot 1 has `owner = 0` (the all-zero pubkey) while the SPL Token program id is `0x900ff7e8…dd06`, so the rule's antecedent — a foreign-owned asset account — genuinely holds on the trace. `UpdateRewardContext::load` appears as a *completed* frame, so neither `Vault::validate` nor the key comparison rejected the input. `spl_token_account_amount` then runs with `<spl_token::state::Account as Pack>::unpack_from_slice` nested inside it and completing: the foreign-owned buffer parsed successfully and yielded an amount. The handler returns `Ok` (`r.is_err(): '0'`).

Crucially, this witness shows the write landing in persisted state, not just acceptance: `v0.num_assets(): '22443'` becomes `v1.num_assets(): '0x300000066'` — a different value — while `v0.num_shares()` and `v1.num_shares()` are both `2`, as expected for a handler that never touches shares. (The `0x3…` rendering is the counterexample printer widening the value past 64 bits; what matters is that the recorded assets changed.) So the handler decoded a balance out of an account the SPL Token program does not own, found it larger than the recorded 22443, and credited the difference to `vault.assets` via `add_token`.

A compounding upstream weakness: `VaultInfo::try_from` carries the comments `// owned by vault program` and `// has discriminant` but implements neither, so the `vault.vault_assets_account` field that the key comparison compares against is not itself guaranteed to have been written by this program — which makes the one check that does exist partly self-referential.
content.impact: `vault.assets` — the protocol's record of backing assets per share — can be set to an arbitrary attacker-chosen value by pointing the reward sync at a fabricated 165-byte token-account-shaped buffer. Inflated assets corrupt the share/asset exchange rate, so subsequent redemptions pay out against assets the vault does not hold, draining real deposits and leaving the vault insolvent (or, symmetrically, mispricing deposits). This is incorrect accounting that directly translates into loss of user funds.
content.attack_path:
1. The attacker creates a 165-byte data account under a program they control (or a System-owned data account) and writes a token-account-shaped layout into it: valid `COption` discriminant tags, `state = 1` (initialized), and an arbitrary large `amount` in bytes 64..72.
2. The vault record's `vault_assets_account` field names that forged account (in the counterexample this is a program-owned vault whose 226 bytes are unconstrained — nothing in the program establishes that the field was written by an honest prior instruction, since `VaultInfo::try_from` performs neither an owner nor a discriminator check).
3. The attacker invokes `process_update_reward`, passing the program-owned vault account and the forged account. No signer is required.
4. `UpdateRewardContext::load` completes: `Vault::validate` passes and the only asset-account guard, the key comparison against `vault.vault_assets_account`, matches.
5. `spl_token_account_amount` unpacks the foreign-owned buffer (`owner = 0`, not the SPL Token program id `0x900ff7e8…dd06`) and returns the attacker-chosen `amount`.
6. `vault_update_reward` computes `reward = new_amt - vault.assets` (new_amt > 22443) and calls `add_token(reward)`; the handler returns `Ok` and the inflated `vault.assets` is persisted (`v0.num_assets() = 22443` → a different `v1.num_assets()`), with `num_shares` unchanged at 2.
content.assumptions_and_uncertainties: The counterexample's vault state account is program-owned by assumption, but its 226 bytes are otherwise unconstrained, so the witness relies on the vault record naming the forged asset account. This is an honest model given that `VaultInfo::try_from` implements neither the owner check nor the discriminator its comments promise, but the trace does not establish that a freshly initialized, honestly written vault can be driven into that state — that is a separate question and is not claimed here. What the trace establishes without qualification is that the handler contributes no owner check on the account whose balance it trusts, and that the resulting inflation is written to persisted state. The `v1.num_assets(): '0x300000066'` rendering exceeds the u64 range; this is the counterexample printer widening the value and affects only how the number reads, not whether the write occurred. This is the only counterexample reviewed; nothing is inferred here about sibling rules in the same batch.

findings.title: `VaultInfo::try_from` omits the vault-account owner check, letting any caller feed forged vault state to `process_update_reward` (and every other vault handler)

content.summary: `VaultInfo::try_from` contains a comment promising an "owned by vault program" check but never performs it; its only guard is `assets_mint != shares_mint`. The Prover produced a trace in which `process_update_reward` accepts a vault state account owned by a foreign program, decodes a balance from an attacker-chosen token account, and returns `Ok` after mutating the forged vault's `assets` field (9298 → 12,884,901,913). Because every vault context (`DepositContext`, `RedeemSharesContext`, `SlashContext`, the fee contexts) loads the vault through the same `TryFrom`, the missing check is a program-wide authentication gap, not a single-handler bug.
content.impact: An unprivileged caller can present an arbitrary account they control as the program's vault state. Every decision made from that state — recognized balance, reward arithmetic, which token account is treated as the vault's assets account — is attacker-chosen. Because the same unchecked `VaultInfo::try_from` is the entry point for the deposit, redeem, slash and fee contexts, which write to accounts the program does own, the gap amounts to a loss of authentication over core vault accounting and is a direct path to corrupted share/asset accounting and theft of vault funds.
content.attack_path:
1. Attacker creates an account of exactly `size_of::<Vault>()` bytes owned by a program other than the vault program (or by the system program), and fills it with bytes of their choosing.
2. They set `assets_mint != shares_mint` in those bytes, which is the only condition `Vault::validate` enforces.
3. They set the forged `vault_assets_account` field to the key of an SPL-Token-owned account they also control and will pass in slot 1, so the self-referential `require_eq!` in `UpdateRewardContext::validate` trivially passes.
4. They invoke `process_update_reward` with the forged vault in slot 0 and their token account in slot 1. `VaultInfo::try_from` never checks `info.owner == crate::ID`, so `UpdateRewardContext::load` succeeds.
5. The handler unpacks a balance from the attacker's token account, computes `reward = balance - vault.assets` using the forged `assets` (9298 in the trace), and credits it via `Vault::add_token`, producing `num_assets = 12,884,901,913`, then returns `Ok`.
6. The same unchecked loader is reachable from `DepositContext`, `RedeemSharesContext`, `SlashContext` and the fee contexts, where the resulting forged state drives transfers out of accounts the program does own.
content.assumptions_and_uncertainties: Two cosmetic artifacts of the trace do not affect the diagnosis: the counterexample renders `vault_info owner` as a value wider than 32 bytes (printer widening, not a real pubkey), and the decoded token balance is not logged directly — it is inferable from `v1.num_assets()`. The Solana runtime will reject the persisted write to a foreign-owned account at the end of the transaction, so the *write-back* shown in this specific trace is not itself durable; the exploitable surface is the read side and, above all, the identical missing check on the handlers that mutate program-owned accounts. Recommended fixes: (1) add `require_eq!(info.owner, &crate::ID, ProgramError::IllegalOwner)` in `VaultInfo::try_from`/`validate`, which closes this for every handler at once; (2) implement the promised account discriminator and bound `data.len() >= size_of::<Vault>()` before the `bytemuck` cast, so the loader is total and a differently-typed program-owned account cannot be read as a `Vault`; (3) have `UpdateRewardContext` call `VaultAssetsAccount::check_vault` (the canonical-PDA re-derivation `DepositContext` and `SlashContext` perform and this context omits) and have `spl_token_account_amount` verify `info.owner == &spl_token::id()` before unpacking — these last two are tracked as a separate property but belong to the same family.

findings.title: update_reward trusts an unvalidated asset account: no canonical PDA re-derivation and no SPL Token owner check, allowing arbitrary inflation of vault.assets

content.summary: `UpdateRewardContext` accepts an arbitrary account as the vault's asset token account: unlike `DepositContext`/`SlashContext`, it never calls `VaultAssetsAccount::check_vault` to re-derive the canonical `[VAULT_ASSETS, vault_pk]` PDA, and `spl_token_account_amount` unpacks the account data without checking that the SPL Token program owns it. The Prover produced an execution where `process_update_reward` returns `Ok` with an asset account whose key differs from the program-derived address, and in the same trace `vault.assets` jumped from 4,612 to 0x300000079 — an attacker-controlled balance written into the vault record as recognized reward.
content.description:
`process_update_reward` reads the vault's asset balance by unpacking SPL token account bytes from the account passed at index 1 and recognizing any surplus over `vault.assets` as reward. The only validation performed on that account is in `UpdateRewardContext::validate`:

```rust
require_eq!(&vault.vault_assets_account, self.vault_assets_account.key, ProgramError::InvalidArgument);
```

This check is self-referential. The right-hand side is the key of whatever account the caller chose to pass; the left-hand side is a field read out of the vault state account's bytes. It therefore proves only "you passed the account the record names" — never "this account is the program's canonical `create_program_address([VAULT_ASSETS, vault_pk], vault.vault_assets_account_bump)` PDA".

Two structural omissions make this exploitable:

1. **No PDA re-derivation.** `UpdateRewardContext` declares the field as a bare `AccountInfo<'info>` rather than the `VaultAssetsAccount<'info>` newtype used by `DepositContext` and `SlashContext`, and loads it with `next_account_info(iter)?.clone()`, bypassing the `TryFrom` path. Because of the field type, `check_vault` — which re-derives the address and compares — is not even reachable, and `UpdateRewardContext::validate` omits the call that both sibling contexts make.

2. **No owner check.** `spl_token_account_amount` is just `spl_token::state::Account::unpack(&info.try_borrow_data()?)`. `Pack::unpack` validates the data length, the `COption` tags and `is_initialized` — it never inspects `info.owner`. So any account whose bytes happen to be shaped like an initialized SPL token account is accepted, regardless of which program owns it.

The counterexample makes the break concrete. The asset account key is `0xc3ff...` while the program's own derivation returns a different value, so the antecedent "non-canonical asset account" genuinely holds on this path. `UpdateRewardContext::load` completes without error, `spl_token_account_amount` → `unpack_from_slice` runs on the forged account, and the handler returns `Ok` (`r.is_err(): '0'`). Critically, the handler does not merely accept the account passively: `v0.num_assets()` is 4,612 before the call and `v1.num_assets()` is `0x300000079` after it, while `num_shares` is unchanged at 9,605. The handler read a balance out of the attacker-supplied account, computed a strictly positive reward, and persisted an attacker-chosen `vault.assets` into the vault record.

One caveat on the strength of the witness, which does not weaken the conclusion: the build summarizes `Pubkey::create_program_address`, so the derived `expected` address printed as `'0'` is unconstrained and is not a plausible real on-chain PDA. What the trace establishes rigorously is the structural fact that is the entire content of the property — the handler's acceptance is independent of *any* program-address derivation, because none is performed anywhere on its path. Under the summary, `expected` could have been any value and the handler would still have returned `Ok`, since no code reads it. The secondary observation — `vault.assets` changing after `unpack_from_slice` ran on the forged account — does not depend on the summary at all and is what demonstrates the consequence.

The exposure is compounded by a related gap the analysis flags: `VaultInfo::try_from` carries the comments `// owned by vault program` and `// has discriminant` but implements neither, performing only `Vault::validate` (`require_ne!(assets_mint, shares_mint)`). This means `vault.vault_assets_account` and `vault.vault_assets_account_bump` — the very inputs a re-derivation would use — can themselves be attacker-chosen, so adding the derivation alone would not be sound without also fixing the vault-account owner and discriminant checks.
content.impact: An attacker can inflate `vault.assets` to an arbitrary value by passing a forged, token-account-shaped account to `update_reward`, causing the vault to recognize phantom reward it never received. Since share price and subsequent redemption accounting are derived from `vault.assets`, this corrupts the vault's core accounting: attacker-held shares can be valued against assets that do not exist, enabling over-redemption against the real asset reserve and leaving the vault insolvent for remaining depositors. The absence of the SPL Token owner check means the "balance" need not come from any real token account at all.
content.attack_path:
1. The attacker constructs (or reuses) an account whose data is shaped like an initialized SPL token account — correct length, valid `COption` tags, `is_initialized` set — and whose `amount` field encodes an arbitrarily large balance. Because `spl_token_account_amount` calls `Pack::unpack` without consulting `info.owner`, this account need not be owned by the SPL Token program.
2. The attacker supplies a vault state account whose `vault_assets_account` field holds the key of that forged account. `VaultInfo::try_from` enforces neither program ownership nor a discriminant, and `Vault::validate` only requires `assets_mint != shares_mint`, so the record is accepted.
3. The attacker invokes `update_reward` with these two accounts. `UpdateRewardContext::load` takes the asset account via `next_account_info(iter)?.clone()` as a bare `AccountInfo`, so `check_vault` is never reachable and no PDA is re-derived.
4. `UpdateRewardContext::validate` runs its single `require_eq!(&vault.vault_assets_account, self.vault_assets_account.key, ...)`, which passes trivially because both sides trace back to the attacker's own inputs.
5. The handler unpacks the forged balance, computes the surplus over the stored `vault.assets` as recognized reward, and persists the inflated value — in the trace, `num_assets` goes from 4,612 to 0x300000079 with `num_shares` unchanged at 9,605, so the handler returns `Ok` with corrupted vault accounting.
content.assumptions_and_uncertainties:
The counterexample was produced under a build that applies a default points-to summary to `Pubkey::create_program_address`, so the derived address printed as `'0'` is unconstrained and the specific pubkey values in the trace are not plausible real on-chain addresses. The violation therefore proves the structural absence of any address derivation on the handler's path rather than a concrete mismatch against a real PDA; this is sufficient, since no code on the path reads the derived value at all. The `vault.assets` corruption observed in the trace does not depend on the summary.

The write-up assumes the standard vault economics in which `vault.assets` feeds share-price and redemption math; the exact downstream loss magnitude depends on the redemption logic, which was not part of this rule. Step 2 of the attack path relies on the separate missing owner/discriminant checks in `VaultInfo::try_from` (the subject of the companion Property 8 rule); even without forging the vault record, the missing owner check in `spl_token_account_amount` remains independently exploitable against whatever account the legitimate record names if that account is ever not a genuine SPL token account.

Recommended remediation, per the analysis: (1) type the field as `VaultAssetsAccount<'info>` and load it via `try_into()`; (2) add `self.vault_assets_account.check_vault(self.vault_info.as_ref().key, &vault)?` to `UpdateRewardContext::validate`; (3) add `require_eq!(info.owner, &spl_token::id(), ProgramError::IllegalOwner)` inside `spl_token_account_amount` before the unpack, so every caller inherits it; (4) add the missing `crate::ID` owner check and discriminant check to `VaultInfo::try_from`, plus a length guard before the `data[0..size_of::<Vault>()]` slice in `get`/`get_mut`, which panics on a short account today.
